strengths: Well-motivated physics-informed design: using the zeroth-step Hamiltonian H(0) (constructed from the initial charge density, no diagonalization needed) as both input descriptor and output prior, so the network learns a correction ΔH, is a sensible and clearly articulated idea that reduces the complexity of the regression target.

The joint R-space/k-space training objective with a physically-grounded PQ cross-subspace penalty is a genuine and well-argued contribution; the error-amplification analysis via the condition number of the overlap matrix (Appendix A.2) and the ghost-state demonstration in ablations (Ablation@Loss-k vs. Ablation@Loss-PQ vs. Full, Fig. 9) convincingly justify the design.

The Materials-HAM-SOC dataset (17,000 structures, 68 elements, six rows, explicit SOC, 4s2p2d1f basis) is a substantial community resource addressing a real scarcity of broad-coverage Hamiltonian benchmarks.
Comprehensive and fine-grained ablation studies (Table 4) that isolate each component, plus a thoughtful gauge-invariant evaluation metric (Gauge MAE) appropriate for the Hamiltonian task.

Strong efficiency evaluation: careful end-to-end timing decomposition (Table 3) showing ~97% wall-clock reduction vs. DFT, with honest discussion of the H(0)-construction bottleneck and scaling caveats.
Extensive band-structure visualizations (Figs. 8-9) supporting physical fidelity of predictions.
weaknesses: No comparison against any external baseline. There is no head-to-head evaluation against existing Hamiltonian predictors (e.g., DeepH-E3, QHNet, Equiformer, DeepH-2, UniMat of Wang et al. 2024b, Zhong et al. 2025, or TraceGrad itself) on the new dataset or any shared benchmark. Consequently it is impossible to determine how much of the reported accuracy comes from the proposed method versus the large curated training set or the H(0) prior; the 'universal and highly accurate' claim is not supported by relative evidence.

Evaluation is confined to the authors' own self-curated dataset. There is no evaluation on established benchmarks (e.g., single-material systems like MoS2/Bi2Se3 used in prior work), so cross-paper comparability and generality claims remain unverified.

Band-structure accuracy is assessed only qualitatively via plots; no quantitative metric (e.g., band MAE in eV, band-gap error) is reported, weakening the claim of 'DFT-level precision' on downstream quantities.

Several components appear incremental or borrowed: the architecture extends Equiformer and TraceGrad, residual prediction is a standard technique, and the ensemble of distance-partitioned sub-models (four separate networks plus a special rule that H(0) is used verbatim beyond 6 Å) adds significant system complexity whose necessity versus a single larger model is only partially addressed by the ensemble ablation.

Statistical rigor is thin: a single fixed random seed (1), single train/test split, and hyperparameters tuned on the validation set with no sensitivity analysis; error bars or variance across seeds/splits are absent, which matters given the small margins between some ablations (e.g., Full 1.417 vs. Ablation@Loss-PQ 1.496 meV, a 5% difference).

Novelty positioning is somewhat overclaimed ('new paradigm', 'breakthrough'); the core ideas (physical priors, equivariant transformers, auxiliary losses) are assembled from known ingredients, and the main novel piece (k-space PQ loss) is only validated on the authors' data.

Practical scope caveats are underplayed in the main text: nonmagnetic compounds only, 6x6x6 k-mesh, PBE/ONCV settings, and testing limited to relatively small cells (mostly 11-30 atoms), which limits evidence for the claimed O(N) scaling advantages on large systems.

strengths: Comprehensive dataset contribution: Materials-HAM-SOC spans 68 elements and explicitly incorporates spin–orbit coupling with fine-grained orbital bases (up to 4s2p2d1f), filling a real gap in open Hamiltonian benchmarks.

The zeroth-step Hamiltonian H(0) as both input descriptor and output prior is a physically motivated idea, and Table 1 convincingly disentangles the contribution of the prior versus the learned correction.
Thorough ablation studies (Appendix A.8) that isolate each component, and a clear error-amplification analysis (Appendix A.2) motivating the k-space and P–Q coupling losses.
End-to-end runtime comparison (Table 3) shows substantial and well-analyzed speedups over the DFT SC loop.
Gauge-invariant evaluation metric and element-wise generalization analysis (Fig. 3) are appropriate for this task.
weaknesses: No direct comparison against existing methods. The paper claims to advance 'universal deep learning for Hamiltonian prediction', yet never benchmarks NextHAM against any competing baseline (e.g., DeepH-2, QHNet, Zhong et al. 2025, TraceGrad) on its own dataset or any standard external benchmark. The reported 1.417 meV error is uninterpretable without context, making the central claim of superiority unsupported.

Limited methodological novelty. The framework is largely an assembly of existing components: TraceGrad (Yin et al., 2025) transplanted into an Equiformer-derived Transformer, residual learning, the gauge-shift trick of Wang et al. (2024b), and a distance-binned model ensemble. Each piece is an incremental extension, and the paper does not provide new theoretical analysis of why the combination should generalize.

The headline 'sub-µeV' SOC accuracy is potentially misleading: Table 1 shows H(0) alone already achieves <0.001 meV on the spin-flip blocks, so this result largely reflects copying the prior rather than learned capability. The paper's own framing ('excellent accuracy... spin-off-diagonal blocks') overstates what the network contributes.

Single random seed (seed = 1) with no variance estimates, error bars, or repeated runs; given only 5.2% improvement of the full method over Ablation@Loss-PQ, the statistical significance of several ablation conclusions is unclear.

Test data are drawn from the same random sample of Materials Project nonmagnetic compounds as training; there is no evaluation of extrapolation to unseen structural prototypes, compositions, or magnetic systems, which weakens the 'universal' claim. Lanthanides/actinides and magnetic materials are excluded entirely—ironically the regimes where SOC matters most.

The k-space loss requires eigendecomposition of ground-truth Hamiltonians and ground-truth eigenbases U(k) at training k-points, adding substantial data-generation and training cost that is never quantified; its practicality for large-scale training is questionable.

The dataset appears distributed only with the method, but reproducibility details (code release, exact data curation/criteria for the 17k structures) are incomplete; hyperparameters (λP, λQ, λPQ, λC) are tuned on the validation set with no sensitivity analysis.

Overwritten and imprecise claims ('new paradigm', 'breakthrough', 'DFT-level precision'), and the writing contains grammatical and typographical errors (e.g., 'methods has offered', inconsistent μ conventions in Eq. 20), which suggests the paper was not carefully polished.

The four-sub-model ensemble partitioned by interatomic distance, plus bypassing correction beyond 6.0 Å, reads more as engineering heuristics than principled design, and multiplies the compute cost of a framework whose selling point is efficiency.

strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: Materials-HAM-SOC with 17,000 structures, 68 elements, explicit SOC, f-orbitals, and complete quantities (zeroth-step Hamiltonians, overlap matrices) is a genuinely valuable community resource; the DFT setup details (pseudopotentials, basis, k-mesh) are documented thoroughly.

The zeroth-step Hamiltonian as both input descriptor and output prior is a physically motivated idea, and Table 1 convincingly quantifies how much it shrinks the effective regression space (96% reduction on the dominant block), with a sound gauge-invariant MAE metric.

The k-space loss with P/Q subspace decomposition and the PQ cross-block penalty is well-motivated by an explicit perturbation analysis (condition-number error amplification, Appendix A.2), and the ghost-state analysis across ablations (Fig. 9) is one of the more compelling demonstrations in the paper.
Comprehensive component-wise ablations (input, output, TraceGrad, ensemble, k-loss, PQ term) under matched training conditions, plus an end-to-end runtime comparison with DFT on identical hardware.
Clear writing and a well-organized treatment of the DFT-to-DL background in the appendix, making the paper accessible to both ML and computational materials audiences.
weaknesses: No comparison against any existing Hamiltonian-prediction method (e.g., DeepH-E3, QHNet, DeepH-2, Equiformer, TraceGrad, or the universal model of Zhong et al. 2025). All quantitative results are self-referential (H(0) prior vs. full model, or internal ablations). For a paper claiming a 'universal' and 'breakthrough' method, the absence of external baselines is the single largest evaluation gap and makes it impossible to judge the methodological advance over prior art.

Novelty is largely incremental and openly derivative: the architecture extends TraceGrad (Yin et al., 2025) to a Transformer backbone; the residual formulation with an initial DFT guess is closely related to Li et al. (2025) for molecules; the distance-interval ensemble of four sub-models is an engineering heuristic rather than a principled contribution, and it multiplies training cost by 4 (one GPU per sub-model), which is not factored into the efficiency claims.

The headline 'sub-µeV' spin-off-diagonal accuracy is trivially inherited from H(0) ≈ H(T) in those blocks (Table 1 shows <0.001 meV before the network), so it overstates the network's contribution; the real signal is the 2.834 meV on the ↑↑ real block, which is not compared to any alternative approach.

Downstream quality is only assessed qualitatively via band-structure plots on selected examples; no quantitative band error metric (e.g., MAE on band energies or band gap errors) is reported, and only a single random seed (fixed to 1) is used with no variance estimates.

Several choices are under-justified: the hyperparameters (e.g., λ_R = 0.99955, λ_P = 0.0002) are tuned on the validation set without sensitivity analysis; the P/Q energy cutoff (10 eV) and the 6.0 Å rule for bypassing the network are empirical rules whose generality across chemistries is untested.

The dataset is drawn only from nonmagnetic compounds, so the claimed generality across 'the full diversity of real-world materials' is overstated; magnetic ordering, which interacts nontrivially with SOC, is excluded. Also, no explicit repository/URL for code and data release is provided despite the release claim.

The efficiency comparison omits the cost of generating the zeroth-step Hamiltonian inputs for new structures in realistic workflows and acknowledges that H(0) construction dominates NextHAM's runtime (55.46 s of 58.47 s mean), which somewhat tempers the practical speedup narrative for very large systems.

strengths: Significant dual contribution: a generalizable Hamiltonian prediction method (NextHAM) and a new large-scale benchmark (Materials-HAM-SOC) with 17,000 structures, 60+ elements, explicit SOC, and fine-grained orbital bases (up to 4s2p2d1f), addressing a real gap since existing datasets (e.g., QH9) cover only molecules/limited elements.

The zeroth-step Hamiltonian H(0) as a physics-informed input descriptor is a well-motivated idea: it is cheap to compute (no diagonalization, matches GNN message-passing scaling), serves as a delta-learning target (∆H), and is shown to reduce the effective regression space by ~96% (Table 1).

The joint R-space/k-space training objective with an explicit P-Q cross-subspace penalty is a novel and physically grounded contribution; the case study (Fig. 4) convincingly shows that small real-space MAE (0.53 meV) can still produce ghost states, and the PQ penalty suppresses them, with downstream benefits for optical conductivity.
Thorough ablation studies (Table 4) showing each component contributes, plus specialized-scenario comparisons on Monolayer Graphene and MoS2 against DeepH-E3 and TraceGrad where the method wins.

Strong reported accuracy (overall Gauge MAE 1.417 meV; sub-µeV for SOC spin-flip blocks), element-wise error analysis across the periodic table, and a detailed efficiency comparison showing ~97% wall-clock reduction vs. DFT.

Reasonably strong appendix coverage: error-amplification analysis via condition number of S(k), loss derivations, dataset construction details, and gauge-freedom handling with an analytic solution for µ.
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparison on the main benchmark: only DeepH-E3 is evaluated, and it reportedly fails to converge (12.6 meV), making the comparison weak; recent universal/competitive models (Zhong et al. 2024, Wang et al. 2024c, Li et al. 2025, Luo et al. 2025, Xia et al. 2025) are discussed but not empirically compared on Materials-HAM-SOC.

Much of the quantitative evidence resides in appendices; the main text contains no direct baseline error table for the main dataset, and headline claims ('universal', 'DFT-level precision') rest largely on in-distribution testing plus a single anecdotal out-of-distribution Ne case, which the authors themselves admit is not rigorous.

Method novelty is incremental: the architecture is primarily an extension of TraceGrad (Yin et al., 2025) into an Equiformer-style Transformer with edge-feature attention, and output conversions reuse the Wigner-Eckart layers of DeepH-E3; the ensemble of four distance-binned sub-models is an engineering choice whose added inference cost is not analyzed.

The cost of the k-space loss is not discussed: computing ground-truth eigenbases P(k), Q(k) and projected blocks at every k-point during training is expensive (eigen-decompositions) and could substantially increase training time relative to R-space-only training; no training-cost comparison is provided.

Dataset scope has caveats not fully acknowledged: only nonmagnetic compounds are included (limiting 'universal' claims), and possible near-duplicate/leakage between Materials Project train/test structures is not addressed; hyperparameters (λP, λQ, λPQ, cutoffs) are tuned on validation without sensitivity analysis.

Reproducibility statement contains blank/unfilled links for code, pretrained models, and the dataset, weakening the reproducibility claim; dataset size (12k training structures) is modest for a 'universal' model and scaling behavior with more data is untested.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely problem: extending deep-learning Hamiltonian prediction toward 'universal' coverage (60+ elements, spin-orbit coupling, f-orbitals), where most prior work is restricted to single materials or small element sets.

The Materials-HAM-SOC benchmark (17,000 DFT structures with SOC, overlap matrices, and zeroth-step Hamiltonians) is a valuable community resource if released as claimed, and fills a real gap compared to molecule-only datasets like QH9.

The joint R-space/k-space training objective, in particular the explicit penalty on the PQ cross-block to suppress 'ghost states', is physically well-motivated and supported by the error-amplification analysis (Appendix F) and qualitative band-structure evidence (Figs. 4, 10).

Comprehensive ablation studies (Appendix L) isolate the contribution of each component (H(0) input, delta-learning target, TraceGrad, ensemble, k-space loss), and the case study on the Ne-containing structure is an interesting, if preliminary, probe of out-of-distribution element generalization.
End-to-end runtime comparison against the full DFT workflow (Table 3) is reported with unusual transparency, including the fact that H(0) construction dominates the inference time.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is largely combinatorial rather than fundamental: the architecture extends TraceGrad (Yin et al., 2025) into an Equiformer-style Transformer, delta-learning is borrowed from prior Δ-ML work, the gauge treatment follows Wang et al. (2024c), and the ensemble-of-distance-bins strategy is a straightforward engineering choice. Each ingredient is well-executed, but the conceptual contribution beyond prior art is modest.

External baselines are surprisingly weak for a paper claiming a 'universal paradigm'. Only DeepH-E3 (2023) and a cut-down TraceGrad variant are compared. Recent competitive systems (e.g., DeepH-2, Zhong et al. 2024, WANet, Uni-Ham, Xia et al. 2025, Luo et al. 2025) are discussed in the related work but not benchmarked. The claim that DeepH-E3 simply 'fails to converge' on the new dataset without evidence of careful hyperparameter tuning makes the 12.6 meV vs 1.4 meV comparison (Table 5) unconvincing.

Statistical rigor is limited: a single random seed (fixed to 1) is used for all reported results, with no error bars or repeated runs, despite the fact that the full-method advantage over the closest ablation is only 5.2% (1.417 vs 1.496 meV). This gap may not be statistically significant.

The k-space loss requires the ground-truth eigenbasis U(k) (i.e., P(k), Q(k) eigenvectors) during training, which substantially increases the training cost and data-storage requirements relative to standard Hamiltonian learning; the paper does not quantify this training overhead, which weakens the claimed efficiency narrative.

The out-of-distribution generalization claim rests on a single Ne-containing test structure. This is anecdotal evidence, and the authors themselves admit that 'further element-level OOD evaluations' are future work; the strong OOD-generalization claims in the abstract/introduction are not supported at this level of evidence.
Reproducibility statement contains blank/placeholder links for code, models, and the dataset ('available here: ,'), which undermines the claimed community contribution at submission time.

Several hyperparameters (λ_P, λ_Q, λ_PQ, cutoff energy for P/Q splitting, distance-bin boundaries for the ensemble) are tuned on the validation set without sensitivity analysis; the design has many degrees of freedom that increase overfitting risk to the benchmark.

The dataset is restricted to nonmagnetic compounds, which somewhat limits the claimed breadth of 'universal' coverage (magnetic/strongly correlated systems are excluded), and this restriction is not prominently discussed relative to the framing.

strengths: Comprehensive contribution on both methodology and data: the Materials-HAM-SOC benchmark (17k structures, 60+ elements, explicit SOC, f-orbital basis) fills a genuine gap, as existing public Hamiltonian datasets (QH9) are molecular-only and small-element.

The zeroth-step Hamiltonian H(0) as a physics-informed input descriptor is a well-motivated idea, clearly grounded in the DFT SCF procedure, and the ablations (Table 4) plus the Table 1 decomposition cleanly quantify how it shrinks the regression target and improves generalization.

The joint R-space/k-space loss with the explicit P–Q cross-block penalty is physically insightful: the paper links the ill-conditioned overlap matrix to error amplification and 'ghost states' (Appendix F), and the band-structure and optical-conductivity case studies (Fig. 4, Fig. 10) convincingly show that real-space MAE alone does not guarantee downstream fidelity.

Strong empirical results: overall Gauge MAE of 1.417 meV, sub-µeV spin-flip blocks, near-perfect band-structure agreement, and large (≈97%) runtime reductions versus full DFT, with an honest breakdown showing the H(0) construction currently dominates inference cost.
Extensive ablation of every proposed component and comparisons against DeepH-E3 and the original TraceGrad on both the new dataset and the MG/MM DeepH benchmarks.
Thorough, largely reproducible documentation: implementation details, hyper-parameters, dataset construction (pseudopotentials, k-mesh, basis sets), and code/data release are promised.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely compositional rather than fundamental: the architecture is an extension of Equiformer attention plus the TraceGrad mechanism (ICML 2025), delta-learning is standard, and the ensemble-by-distance-range split is an engineering device (four separately trained sub-models) that adds complexity and limits elegance.

Heavy reliance on the appendix: the main text contains essentially one results table; key baseline comparisons (Tables 5, 7) and the full ablations are deferred to the appendix, weakening the main-text evidence.

The OOD-generalization claim rests on a single Ne-containing test structure and is acknowledged by the authors as needing further evaluation; this claim should not appear so prominently in the abstract/positioning.

The DeepH-E3 comparison (Table 5) reports 'failure to converge' on the new dataset after moderate modifications; without tuning details, learning-rate schedules, and compute parity, it is hard to rule out implementation/optimization artifacts rather than a fundamental limitation of the baseline.
Single-run evaluation with a fixed random seed; no error bars or variance across seeds, although differences between some ablations (e.g., Full 1.417 vs Loss-PQ 1.496) are small.

The analytical gauge parameter µ derivation (Eqs. 27–28) is convoluted and contains notational irregularities (e.g., the μ²δαβ terms in the k-space contribution), and the explanation of why loss_T can be dropped in the derivation is somewhat hand-wavy.

The reproducibility statement contains blank link placeholders; dataset license, hosting, and long-term availability are unclear. Dataset is restricted to nonmagnetic PBE structures, limiting coverage of strongly correlated and magnetic systems the model is implicitly marketed for.
Multiple hand-set loss hyper-parameters (λ_P, λ_Q, λ_PQ, λ_C, λ_R) tuned on validation; sensitivity analysis for these is not reported.
